title: Edit distance
label: idb-list
statement: Given two words, return the **fewest operations** that turn the first into the second, where one operation inserts a character, deletes a character, or replaces a character.
provenance: **InterviewDB-listed.** LeetCode 72 is on the LinkedIn list you supplied from InterviewDB. No candidate report of this exact question was found in the research passes — the evidence is that the list names it. On that list it is a variation of InterviewDB Q8. Q8 fixes the cost model to one substitution per step and asks for the shortest path, so it is BFS. 72 allows insert, delete and replace and asks for a distance, so it is DP. Q8’s third follow-up - letters may be added or removed - is exactly the bridge: adjacency becomes "edit distance 1", and the dictionary graph now links words of different lengths.

prompts.label: Check my design — no code
prompts.text: I believe d(i, j) = d(i−1, j−1) when the letters match, else 1 + min(replace, delete, insert); fill row by row keeping only the previous row — O(n·m) time, O(m) memory. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Given two words, return the **fewest operations** that turn the first into the second, where one operation inserts a character, deletes a character, or replaces a character.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Do all three operations cost 1? (Yes.)
- Case-sensitive? (Yes.)
- How long are the words? (Up to a few thousand — O(n·m) is fine.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Let d(i, j) be the distance between the first i letters of a and the first j of b. If the last letters match, d(i, j) = d(i−1, j−1). Otherwise it is 1 + the best of replace d(i−1, j−1), delete d(i−1, j) and insert d(i, j−1). Each row needs only the row above it.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: I would say, before coding: "D."(i, j) = d(i−1, j−1) when the letters match, else 1 + min(replace, delete, insert); fill row by row keeping only the previous row — O(n·m) time, O(m) memory."

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Make the design decision yourself, then ask the assistant to attack it.
- Delegate the mechanical parts only after the structure is fixed.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe d(i, j) = d(i−1, j−1) when the letters match, else 1 + min(replace, delete, insert); fill row by row keeping only the previous row — O(n·m) time, O(m) memory. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call MinOps concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Greedy matching of letters — fails on simple cases.
- Plain recursion without memoisation — exponential.
- A full n × m table when two rows are enough (memory O(m)).
- Off-by-one between string index i−1 and table index i.
